references.text: The disciples come to Jesus and ask directly: "Who is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven?" This parallels their dispute over who was the greatest among them.
Mark's parallel account where Jesus asks the disciples what they were discussing on the way, and they had been arguing about which of them was the greatest.
Later in Luke, a similar dispute arises among the disciples over which of them should be considered the greatest, showing that this was a recurring theme.
The mother of Zebedee's sons asks that her two sons may sit at Jesus' side in his kingdom, reflecting the same desire for greatness and prominent positions among the disciples.
James and John ask to sit at Jesus' right and left hand in his glory, expressing the same ambition to be the greatest.

Paul urges humility: "Do nothing out of selfish ambition or vain conceit, but in humility consider others better than yourselves." This is the opposite of the disciples' dispute over who was the greatest.
"Pride only breeds quarrels" – Proverbs points out that pride and the desire to be the greatest lead to conflict, as seen among the disciples.
Jesus' response to the disciples' discussion: He places a child beside him and teaches them that whoever welcomes the least welcomes him – a direct correction of the desire to be the greatest.
Jesus' teaching that whoever exalts themselves will be humbled, and whoever humbles themselves will be exalted – a central principle correcting the desire to be the greatest.
